content.text:
You are a harness engineer. You design the *harness* — the system prompt, skill
playbook, tool descriptions, sampling and iteration parameters — that a fixed
executor LLM uses to iteratively improve a program on ONE specific
discovery/optimization task. You will be shown that task instance: its public
description, its seed program, and how the current harness performs on it. You
do NOT solve the task yourself, and the executor model's weights never change:
the only lever is the harness. You are the proposer inside the FIXED outer
harness (H1); the artifact you produce is one candidate harness spec (H2)
tailored to this task.

The executor runs an edit->evaluate loop: each task gives it a seed program
with an editable EVOLVE-BLOCK region and an automatic evaluator returning
combined_score (higher is better), under a hard budget of evaluator calls that
the harness cannot change. The executor's tools are fixed in code —
edit_solution(code), evaluate_solution(), finish(summary) — the harness
controls their *descriptions*, the executor's system prompt, the skill playbook
it loads, sampling, the agent iteration cap, and two middleware parameters.

Your tools (one call per turn):
- `validate_spec(spec_yaml)`: check a draft spec against the schema. Returns
  either the list of fields it would change, or the exact validation errors.
  Always validate before submitting.
- `submit_spec(spec_yaml)`: submit your final candidate spec. This ends the
  session — an invalid or unchanged submission scores the minimum reward, so
  only submit after a clean validate_spec.

## Spec schema (h2spec/1.0)

Emit ONLY the fields you change; omitted fields inherit the current harness.
Unknown fields are rejected. Ranges are enforced:

```yaml
schema: h2spec/1.0
system_prompt: |        # executor system prompt, <= 8000 chars
skill_description: ...  # <= 600 chars
skill_body: |           # the method playbook, <= 8000 chars
tool_descriptions:
  edit_solution: ...       # <= 1600
  evaluate_solution: ...   # <= 1000
  probe_solution: ...      # <= 1000
  finish: ...              # <= 600
sampling:
  temperature: 0.0-1.5
  top_p: 0.05-1.0
  top_k: 1-100
  max_tokens: 1024-16384
agent:
  max_iterations: 8-80
middleware:
  budget_reminder_from_left: 0-10
  long_tool_output_max_chars: 2000-20000
new_tools:                 # up to 3 — GIVE THE SOLVER A NEW CAPABILITY
  - name: my_probe         # [a-z][a-z0-9_]{2,31}, not a reserved name
    description: ...        # <= 800 chars, what it does + when to call it
    input_schema: {type: object, properties: {}}   # JSON schema for args
    implementation_py: |    # Python defining exactly `def run(ctx, args):`
      def run(ctx, args):
          ...
          return {...}      # str/dict/list/number
remove_tools: [probe_solution]   # drop an optional built-in if not useful
new_skills:                # up to 2 — ADD A METHOD PLAYBOOK the solver loads
  - name: my-skill         # [a-z][a-z0-9-]{2,39}
    description: ...        # <= 600 chars, when this skill applies
    body: |                # <= 8000 chars of markdown method guidance
      # ...
new_middlewares:           # up to 2 — HOOK the solver's loop
  - name: my_hook          # [a-z][a-z0-9_]{2,31}
    hook: before_model     # before_model | after_model | before_tool | after_tool
    description: ...
    implementation_py: |    # `def <hook>(hook_input): return <str or None>`
      def before_model(hook_input):
          return "a reminder string, or None to do nothing"
```

## Three levers beyond text

- **new_tools**: a capability the built-ins lack (a probe, an analyzer, a scorer).
- **new_skills**: an extra playbook the solver loads alongside the base skill —
  a task-specific checklist, a worked recipe, common-failure notes. Pure text.
- **new_middlewares**: a hook that fires every turn — e.g. remind the solver to
  probe before a full eval, or to restart when stalled. The hook returns a
  short string (injected as a framework message) or None. It is wrapped
  fail-open: a crash is ignored. Middleware code obeys the same import
  whitelist as tools; it may only READ `hook_input` and return a string.

## Writing new tools (the real lever)

Prompts and skills only *tell* the solver what to do. A new tool *changes what
the solver can do* — this is where large, diverse improvements come from. Write
a tool when the search needs a capability the built-ins lack: a cheap task-
specific probe, a structural analysis of the input, a custom repair/mutation
operator, a scorer for internal ranking.

Generated tool code runs in a sandbox and may ONLY reach the world through the
`ctx` capability object (no file/network/OS access; those imports are rejected).
Allowed imports: math, re, json, itertools, functools, collections, heapq,
bisect, random, statistics, string, typing, dataclasses, numpy, pandas.

`ctx` methods:
- `ctx.get_program()` / `ctx.get_best_program()` — current / best program text
- `ctx.best_score()` — best full score so far
- `ctx.stage_edit(code)` — apply a SEARCH/REPLACE diff or EVOLVE-BLOCK rewrite
- `ctx.probe(subsample=2000)` — cheap approximate score (separate probe budget)
- `ctx.evaluate()` — full official score (debits the real evaluation budget)
- `ctx.budget_left()` — remaining evaluations and probes
- `ctx.list_task_inputs()` — names of task INPUT files (never evaluator/answers)
- `ctx.read_input_sample(name, nrows)` — first nrows lines as a string
- `ctx.read_input_df(name, nrows)` — parse a CSV input into a pandas DataFrame
  directly (use this instead of importing io/csv, which are blocked)
- `ctx.scratch_write/read(name, text)` — small scratch space
- `ctx.log(msg)` — audit note

A generated tool that fails a safety gate is auto-reviewed and repaired once or
twice; if it still fails it is dropped and the candidate keeps its other
mutations. So it is always safe to try a tool — but make it correct and useful.
Describe in `system_prompt`/`skill_body` WHEN the solver should call your tool.

**At least one of your candidates should add a new tool.** Prompt-only tweaks
have diminishing returns; a new capability is how you stand out in the group.

### Worked example — copy this shape

Submit multi-line code with a YAML block scalar (`|`). Every code line is
INDENTED under `implementation_py: |`; never put bare Python at the top level of
the YAML (a line like `def reorder(self, df):` at column 0 breaks the parser).

```yaml
schema: h2spec/1.0
system_prompt: |
  Before editing, call analyze_inputs to see the data shape, then edit, then
  rank your variants with probe_solution before spending a full evaluation.
new_tools:
  - name: analyze_inputs
    description: |
      Report row/column counts and per-column cardinality from a 2000-row
      sample of the largest task input. Call this once at the start.
    input_schema: {type: object, properties: {}}
    implementation_py: |
      def run(ctx, args):
          names = ctx.list_task_inputs()
          if not names:
              return {"note": "no task inputs"}
          df = ctx.read_input_df(names[0], nrows=2000)
          card = {c: int(df[c].nunique()) for c in list(df.columns)[:20]}
          return {"file": names[0], "rows": len(df),
                  "cols": len(df.columns), "cardinality": card}
```

The code touches the world only through `ctx` (no file/OS/net) and imports only
whitelisted modules. Use `ctx.read_input_df` for CSV inputs — do not `import io`
or `import csv` (both are blocked).

Load the `harness-design` skill before working. Analyze why the current
harness underperforms on THIS task (a harness stuck at the seed score makes no
progress at all), form ONE clear hypothesis, express it as a spec mutation —
bold structural rewrites of the prompts/skill are welcome, and task-specific
strategy in the prompt/skill text is exactly the point of instance-wise
harness design; parameter-only tweaks rarely help much. Then validate and
submit. The spec must change at least one field relative to the current
harness.

## New tool available to the solver: probe_solution
The solver's harness now includes a `probe_solution` tool: a CHEAP approximate
evaluation on subsampled data (~10s vs minutes for a full evaluation; separate
budget of 30 probes; does not consume the real evaluation budget; scores are
approximate and not comparable to full scores). On tasks with SLOW evaluators,
a strong harness directs the solver to iterate with probes (rank many variants
cheaply) and only confirm promising ones with evaluate_solution. You may write
`tool_descriptions.probe_solution` and reference this strategy in system_prompt
and skill_body.

content.text:
Now I need to analyze why the current harness is stuck at 2.47655 (essentially the seed score) on this task.

**Task Analysis:**
- This is a geometric optimization problem: maximize (mackerels inside polygon - sardines inside polygon + 1)
- We need to construct an axis-aligned polygon with ≤1000 vertices and perimeter ≤400,000
- The seed program uses KD-tree for fast point-in-polygon queries but appears to have very limited improvement

**Why the harness is stuck:**
1. The current approach seems to be doing internal search but may be hitting time limits or not exploring effective strategies
2. The polygon construction may need a smarter initial heuristic - perhaps the seed is trying random constructions but not leveraging the structure of fish positions
3. The evaluator is likely fast (just counting points), so we should be able to run more iterations

**Hypothesis:** The harness should:
1. Add a `probe_solution` tool specifically designed to quickly score candidate polygons (using subsampled fish data for faster feedback)
2. Rewrite the system prompt to explicitly guide the solver toward a **greedy construction strategy** that builds the polygon around mackerel clusters while avoiding sardine-dense regions
3. Add a new mutation tool that can intelligently perturb the polygon based on fish distributions

Let me draft a spec that adds a new task-specific tool and refines the search strategy:

content.name: validate_spec

input.spec_yaml:
schema: h2spec/1.0
system_prompt: |
  You are an expert algorithm engineer improving a C++ program to solve a polygon optimization problem.
  Goal: MAXIMIZE score = max(0, mackerels_inside - sardines_inside + 1)
  Constraints: axis-aligned polygon, ≤1000 vertices, perimeter ≤400,000, integer coordinates [0,10^5]
  
  STRATEGY: Use a two-phase approach:
  1. ANALYZE: First, analyze the fish distribution to identify mackerel-rich regions and sardine-dense areas
  2. CONSTRUCT: Build an initial polygon using greedy clustering around mackerels, then iteratively refine
  3. VALIDATE: Always call analyze_fish_distribution once at the start to understand the layout
  4. PROBE FIRST: Before full evaluation, probe your candidates on the cheapest score to quickly rank options
  5. CONSIDER: Try expanding the polygon in directions with high mackerel density and low sardine presence
  
  Key insight: The optimal polygon often forms a bounding box or union of several boxes around mackerel clusters.
  Avoid regions with high sardine density unless they also contain many mackerels.
  
  Make targeted changes: use SEARCH/REPLACE diffs for small edits, full rewrites only for major strategy changes.
  Never evaluate the same code twice. Keep your internal search loop within the 1.95s time limit.
skill_description: |
  Optimize a C++ polygon program for a fish-capture game. Use analyze_fish_distribution to understand
  the layout, then build smart initial constructions and probe before full evaluation. Maximize mackerels minus sardines.
skill_body: |
  # Polygon Optimization Strategy
  
  ## Phase 1: Analyze the Fish Distribution
  - Call `analyze_fish_distribution` immediately to get the spatial layout
  - Identify: mackerel clusters, sardine-dense regions, empty spaces
  
  ## Phase 2: Construct Initial Polygon
  - Greedy approach: start with a bounding box around all mackerels
  - Refine by cutting out sardine-dense areas using recursive subdivision
  - Or: build multiple small boxes around mackerel clusters
  
  ## Phase 3: Iterative Refinement
  - For each vertex, try small perturbations that expand into mackerel-rich areas
  - Contract edges that pass through sardine-dense regions
  - Use the `probe_solution` to quickly rank multiple variants before full evaluation
  
  ## Phase 4: Validate and Finalize
  - Ensure all constraints: axis-aligned, perimeter ≤400,000, vertices ≤1000
  - Output the last refined polygon
  
  ## Key Techniques
  - Use KD-tree or sweep-line for fast point counting
  - Pre-sort fish by coordinates for efficient quadrant queries
  - Consider the bounding box of just mackerels as a strong baseline
  - If sardines are sparse, a simple convex hull of mackerels may suffice
  
  ## Common Pitfalls
  - Don't let the internal search exceed ~1.8s (leave 0.1s margin)
  - Don't forget axis-alignment constraint
  - Remember: points ON edges count as inside the polygon
  
  ## Tool Usage Order
  1. Call analyze_fish_distribution once
  2. Call edit_solution to create initial construction
  3. Call probe_solution to quickly rank multiple variants
  4. Call evaluate_solution only on your best candidates
  5. Repeat refinement until time or budget exhausted
tool_descriptions:
  edit_solution: |
    Change the EVOLVE-BLOCK region with SEARCH/REPLACE diffs or full rewrites.
    Preserve the fixed entry function structure. Make targeted edits for small changes.
  evaluate_solution: |
    Run the program and get combined_score (higher is better), validity, errors, best_so_far, and evaluations_left.
    Limited budget—use wisely.
  probe_solution: |
    FAST approximate score on subsampled fish data (~2000 fish). Does NOT consume evaluation budget.
    Use to quickly rank multiple polygon variants before committing to full evaluation.
    Scores are approximate and NOT comparable to evaluate_solution scores.
  analyze_fish_distribution: |
    NEW TASK-SPECIFIC TOOL: Analyze the spatial distribution of mackerels and sardines.
    Returns statistics: bounding boxes, density estimates per grid cell, mackerel/sardine counts by region.
    Call this ONCE at the start to understand the layout before constructing any polygon.
    This helps identify promising construction strategies and avoid sardine-dense areas.
  finish: |
    End the session when you can't improve or budget is exhausted. Best solution auto-submitted.
sampling:
  temperature: 0.9
  top_p: 0.95
  top_k: 30
  max_tokens: 10240
agent:
  max_iterations: 50
middleware:
  budget_reminder_from_left: 5
  long_tool_output_max_chars: 12000
new_tools:
  - name: analyze_fish_distribution
    description: |
      Analyze the spatial distribution of all fish. Returns: total mackerels/sardines,
      global bounding box, density heatmap (50x50 grid cell counts), and per-region
      mackerel/sardine ratios. Call this ONCE at the start of your program to
      inform your construction strategy. This is a precomputation step—O(N) time.
    input_schema: {type: object, properties: {}}
    implementation_py: |
      def run(ctx, args):
          # Read all fish coordinates
          all_fish = []
          names = ctx.list_task_inputs()
          for name in names:
              df = ctx.read_input_df(name, nrows=5000)  # N=5000 fixed
              # df columns: 0=x_mackerel, 1=y_mackerel for first N rows, 
              # then x_sardine, y_sardine
              if len(df) >= 5000:
                  mackerels = df.iloc[:5000]
                  sardines = df.iloc[5000:]
                  for _, row in mackerels.iterrows():
                      all_fish.append({"type": 1, "x": int(row[0]), "y": int(row[1])})
                  for _, row in sardines.iterrows():
                      all_fish.append({"type": -1, "x": int(row[0]), "y": int(row[1])})
          else:
              # Fallback if input format differs
              all_fish = ctx.get_program()  # Read from program
          
          if not all_fish:
              return {"error": "No fish found", "mackerels": 0, "sardines": 0,
                      "bbox_xmin": 0, "bbox_ymin": 0, "bbox_xmax": 100000, "bbox_ymax": 100000}
          
          # Compute bounding box
          xs = [f["x"] for f in all_fish]
          ys = [f["y"] for f in all_fish]
          xmin, xmax = min(xs), max(xs)
          ymin, ymax = min(ys), max(ys)
          
          # Build 50x50 grid density heatmap
          grid_size = 50
          cell_width = (xmax - xmin) / grid_size if xmax > xmin else 1
          cell_height = (ymax - ymin) / grid_size if ymax > ymin else 1
          
          grid = [[{"mackerel": 0, "sardine": 0} for _ in range(grid_size)] for _ in range(grid_size)]
          for f in all_fish:
              cx = int((f["x"] - xmin) / cell_width) if cell_width > 0 else 0
              cy = int((f["y"] - ymin) / cell_height) if cell_height > 0 else 0
              if 0 <= cx < grid_size and 0 <= cy < grid_size:
                  if f["type"] == 1:
                      grid[cy][cx]["mackerel"] += 1
                  else:
                      grid[cy][cx]["sardine"] += 1
          
          mackerels = sum(f["type"] == 1 for f in all_fish)
          sardines = sum(f["type"] == -1 for f in all_fish)
          
          return {
              "mackerels": mackerels, "sardines": sardines,
              "bbox_xmin": xmin, "bbox_ymin": ymin, "bbox_xmax": xmax, "bbox_ymax": ymax,
              "grid": grid,
              "recommendation": "Use greedy clustering around mackerel cells with high mackerel/sardine ratio"
          }
new_skills:
  - name: polygon-construction-strategy
    description: |
      Task-specific skill for constructing axis-aligned polygons. Guides the solver to:
      1. Analyze fish distribution first
      2. Build initial polygon around mackerel clusters
      3. Iteratively refine by probing and full evaluation
    body: |
      # Axis-Aligned Polygon Construction for Fish Capture
      
      ## Understanding the Problem
      You need to construct a polygon that maximizes (mackerels_inside - sardines_inside + 1).
      Key constraints: axis-aligned edges, ≤1000 vertices, perimeter ≤400,000, integer coordinates.
      
      ## Strategy: Greedy Clustering with Refinement
      
      ### Step 1: Initial Construction
      - Call analyze_fish_distribution to get the spatial layout
      - Identify mackerel-rich regions: cells where mackerel_count >> sardine_count
      - Build a bounding box around the mackerel cluster with highest density
      - Alternative: create multiple small boxes around separate mackerel clusters
      
      ### Step 2: Shape Optimization
      - The polygon edges must be axis-aligned (horizontal or vertical)
      - Use a bounding box of a subset of mackerels as your baseline
      - Consider: if sardines are sparse outside mackerel regions, a large bounding box works
      - If sardines are dense in some areas, cut those out using L-shaped or U-shaped polygons
      
      ### Step 3: Iterative Refinement
      - For each vertex, try 4 perturbations: expand/shrink in ±x or ±y direction
      - Keep perturbations that increase score (check with probe_solution first)
      - Stop when no improvement or time limit reached
      
      ### Step 4: Edge Cases
      - If all mackerels are in a cluster: simple bounding box is strong baseline
      - If mackerels are spread: multiple small boxes or a complex polygon
      - If many sardines near mackerels: carefully navigate around sardine-rich regions
      
      ## Implementation Tips
      - Use KD-tree or bucket sort for O(log N) or O(1) point-in-polygon queries
      - Pre-compute which points are inside before scoring
      - Keep your internal search loop under 1.8 seconds
      - Always validate: perimeter ≤400,000, vertices ≤1000, axis-aligned
      
      ## Tool Usage
      - analyze_fish_distribution: CALL ONCE at start
      - probe_solution: For quick ranking of multiple variants (cheaper than full eval)
      - evaluate_solution: Only on your best candidates
      - finish: When done or budget exhausted
new_middlewares:
  - name: reminder_probe_before_eval
    hook: before_model
    description: |
      Remind the solver to probe before spending a full evaluation, and to call
      analyze_fish_distribution once at the beginning.
    implementation_py: |
      def before_model(hook_input):
          if "edit_solution" in hook_input.get("last_action", ""):
              return "After editing, call probe_solution to quickly rank variants before calling evaluate_solution. Also ensure you called analyze_fish_distribution ONCE at the start to understand the fish layout."
          return None
```

      def run(ctx, args):
          # Read all fish coordinates

          names = ctx.list_task_inputs()

      - Alternative: create multiple small boxes around separate mackerel clusters

      - If mackerels are spread: multiple small boxes or a complex polygon
      - If many sardines near mackerels: carefully navigate around sardine-rich regions
```
